books.title: Decisive
books.author: Chip Heath and Dan Heath
needsHumanCheck: Chapter titles and examples may vary by edition. The WRAP framework is confirmed by the authors' official book description and published reviews.
books.hook: Better decisions require more than careful thinking; they require a process that challenges the way we choose.

page1.inOneMinute: Decisive examines why people make poor choices even when they try to think carefully. Chip Heath and Dan Heath identify narrow options, confirmation bias, short-term emotions, and overconfidence as common obstacles. They present the WRAP process: Widen your options, Reality-test your assumptions, Attain distance before deciding, and Prepare to be wrong. The method encourages people to consider alternatives, gather outside evidence, separate immediate emotion from deeper priorities, and plan for uncertainty. The goal is not perfect certainty but a more reliable decision process.
youWillGet: Recognize common traps in personal and business decisions.
page1.whoFor: This book suits readers making difficult career, business, relationship, or personal choices. It is particularly useful for people who repeatedly overthink decisions or become attached to their first idea.

glance.mainIdea: A structured process helps people counter predictable biases when making decisions.
glance.problem: Narrow options, biased evidence, emotion, and overconfidence distort important choices.
glance.promise: The WRAP framework provides practical steps for making decisions more carefully.

inside.line: Escape false either-or choices by considering additional possibilities and opportunity costs.
Seek evidence that challenges your beliefs instead of collecting only supporting information.
Reduce the influence of short-term feelings by examining priorities and taking perspective.
Plan for uncertain outcomes and establish ways to adjust after a decision.

story.heading: Why choices go wrong
story.text: The Heath brothers begin with common errors in decision-making. People restrict themselves to a small set of choices, seek evidence that supports an existing belief, and let immediate emotions dominate. Confidence can also hide uncertainty. Knowing about these problems is not enough; people need a repeatable process that changes how they make decisions.

story.heading: Widen the options
story.text: The first WRAP step challenges narrow choices. Instead of asking which of two options is better, look for alternatives and consider what each option prevents you from doing. The authors encourage readers to escape the first frame of a problem. A wider set of choices often reveals opportunities that the original question concealed.

story.heading: Test assumptions and gain distance
story.text: The next steps focus on evidence and perspective. Reality-testing means gathering information that could prove an assumption wrong. Attaining distance means avoiding a decision based entirely on the emotion of the moment. The authors encourage people to consider broader priorities, seek outside views, and examine what they would advise someone else in the same situation.

story.heading: Prepare for uncertainty
story.text: The final step recognizes that the future remains uncertain even after careful thought. People should consider possible outcomes, define warning signs, and plan how to respond if circumstances change. The framework does not promise perfect predictions. It creates a more deliberate way to choose, act, and revise decisions as new evidence appears.

author: Chip Heath is a professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business. His research and writing examine how ideas spread, how people communicate, and how organizations make decisions. He has coauthored several books with his brother Dan Heath, including Made to Stick and Switch. Their work turns findings from psychology and organizational behavior into practical methods for everyday use.

Dan Heath is an author whose work focuses on organizational change, decision-making, and the ways people solve problems. He has collaborated with Chip on books about communication, change, and significant experiences. In Decisive, the brothers apply research on judgment and decision-making to the choices people face at work and in personal life. Their emphasis is on building a process that counters predictable errors rather than trusting confidence alone.
quickFacts: The book's subtitle is How to Make Better Choices in Life and Work.
The authors are brothers Chip Heath and Dan Heath.
The book introduces the WRAP decision-making framework.

lessons.title: Widen your options
lessons.text: The first WRAP step challenges narrow either-or choices. Look for additional paths, including combinations or alternatives outside the original question. Opportunity cost means what you give up by choosing one option instead of another. A wider view makes those trade-offs easier to see.
lessons.example: When offered a new job, Nisha thinks she must accept or resign from her current role. She also explores a transfer, a revised workload, and a later start date.

lessons.title: Reality-test your assumptions
lessons.text: People naturally search for evidence that supports their preferred answer. Reality-testing deliberately looks for information that could challenge it. Try a small experiment, seek an independent view, or examine what happened in comparable situations before making a major commitment.
lessons.example: Rahul believes customers dislike his new product design. He interviews a few users and tests two versions before spending money on a full redesign.

lessons.title: Attain distance before deciding
lessons.text: Immediate emotion can make a temporary feeling seem like the whole truth. Distance means stepping back to consider deeper goals, values, and the advice you would give another person. The purpose is not to eliminate emotion but to keep it from controlling the entire decision.
lessons.example: After an argument with her manager, Aditi wants to resign that afternoon. She waits, reviews her long-term goals, and decides what information she needs before acting.

lessons.title: Prepare to be wrong
lessons.text: A decision remains exposed to uncertainty even when the reasoning is strong. Prepare for a range of outcomes instead of assuming the preferred result will happen. Identify warning signs, fallback options, and points when you should reconsider the plan.
lessons.example: Before opening a small cafe, Aman defines a spending limit and a date for reviewing customer demand. He prepares a smaller operating plan if sales disappoint.

lessons.title: Use small experiments
lessons.text: When a choice is uncertain, a limited test can provide better information than extended speculation. An experiment makes an assumption observable before a full commitment. It also allows a person to learn from results without bearing the complete cost of an untested plan.
lessons.example: Before switching careers, Meera takes a weekend course and completes a small freelance project. She uses the experience to judge whether the work suits her interests.

lessons.title: Look beyond immediate feelings
lessons.text: Decisive encourages readers to separate short-term emotional reactions from the larger questions that matter. A choice that feels satisfying today may conflict with a long-term priority. Reviewing goals and seeking an outside perspective gives decisions a broader context.
lessons.example: At midnight, Vikram wants to buy an expensive phone after seeing a friend's new device. He waits until the next day and compares the purchase with his savings goal.

remember: A forced choice may hide better alternatives.
Search for evidence that could prove you wrong.
Temporary emotion should not decide every major choice.
Use small tests when a full commitment is risky.
Choose with your deeper priorities in view.
page4.bigIdea: Better decisions come from changing the decision process, not simply thinking harder about the same narrow choices.
mistakes: Collecting information only to support a preferred option instead of testing its weaknesses.
Assuming that careful analysis removes uncertainty or guarantees a successful outcome.

exercises.title: Apply the WRAP process
steps: Write down the decision you need to make.
List additional options beyond your first two choices.
Identify an assumption and find evidence that tests it.
Set a review point and prepare for an unexpected result.

exercises.title: Run a small test
steps: Choose one uncertain belief about your decision.
Design a small, low-cost way to test it.
Decide what result would support or challenge your belief.
Use the result to refine your next step.

exercises.title: Gain perspective
steps: Write down your immediate emotional reaction.
Ask what you would advise a friend in this situation.
Compare that advice with your preferred choice.

page6.whoShouldRead: Read this book if you face complicated decisions and want a practical framework for checking your reasoning. It suits managers, entrepreneurs, students, and anyone weighing important alternatives.
page6.whoMightSkip: You may prefer a technical psychology text if you want detailed academic analysis of decision research. Readers looking for a simple list of rules without reflection or testing may not use the framework fully.

buy.suits: Buy the physical book if you want the extended examples and explanations behind the WRAP framework.
buy.notSuits: Skip it if this overview gives you a process you are ready to apply to your current decision.
buy.physicalGives: The complete book develops the framework through additional cases, experiments, and examples from work and personal life.
